title: The Arithmetic of Spectra: Factorization, Statistics, and Symmetric Functions
abstract: We study factorizations of the single-particle spectrum of non-interacting quantum systems and their consequences for many-particle statistics. Representing the single-particle partition function by a spectral alphabet, tensor factorizations become multiplicative factorizations of the alphabet, which can be lifted to canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions using standard symmetric-function and $λ$-ring identities. We show how product spectra arise from different factorizations, how antisymmetrization can be assigned across an odd number of factors, and which tensor factorizations are compatible with a fixed spectrum. The paper therefore studies spectral factorization and provides a consolidated combinatorial framework for canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions.
summary: This paper develops a combinatorial framework by studying how the single-particle spectrum of non-interacting quantum systems can be factorized. It uses symmetric function theory to derive explicit, related formulas for the canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions. This provides a systematic mathematical tool for understanding quantum statistics based on the underlying spectral structure.
main_problem: The paper studies the factorization properties of the single-particle spectrum of non-interacting quantum systems and how these factorizations determine the resulting many-particle Bose and Fermi statistics.
main_result: It establishes a consolidated combinatorial framework showing that product spectra lead to specific, related forms for the canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions, linking them via symmetric function identities and descent set complementation.
method: The authors use spectral factorization, mapping tensor factorizations of the single-particle kernel to multiplicative factorizations of a formal alphabet, and employing advanced symmetric function theory (Schur functions, $\lambda$-rings).
model_or_system: The analysis is general for non-interacting systems, initially focusing on the imaginary-time propagator ($e^{- eta H_1}$) but generalizing to arbitrary trace-class one-particle kernels $K$. Specific examples include harmonic traps and separable energy spectra.
key_observables: Canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions ($Z_{n,B}, Z_{n,F}$), the single-particle partition function $Z_1( eta)$, and the spectral alphabet $X$.
important_parameters: The dimensionality $d$ of the system (especially for harmonic traps), and the temperature parameter $ eta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability to factorize the spectral alphabet $X$ into simpler components ($\hat{X}, \hat{Y}$), and the mathematical framework is built upon identities derived from the underlying spectral structure.
figures_summary: The notes mention specific identities (Cauchy identities, dual Cauchy identities) and relationships involving major indices ($	ext{maj}(D)$) for harmonic traps, distinguishing between bosonic and fermionic sums.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the spectral factorization framework, establishing the relationship between Bose and Fermi statistics via descent sets, and then applying these concepts to specific physical models like the harmonic trap and general separable systems.
why_interesting: The deep connection between spectral factorization, combinatorial identities (symmetric functions), and the fundamental difference between Bose and Fermi statistics provides a powerful, unified mathematical tool for analyzing quantum many-body systems.
